title: Newton–Girard Identities for the Cubic
description: Proves the Newton–Girard identities for three quantities a, b, c over an arbitrary commutative ring: the power sums pₙ = aⁿ+bⁿ+cⁿ satisfy the linear recurrence pₙ₊₃ = e₁pₙ₊₂ − e₂pₙ₊₁ + e₃pₙ in the elementary symmetric functions, with explicit closed forms for p₁..p₄ and a specialization to the depressed cubic of the parent (e₁ = 0) giving pₙ₊₃ = −p·pₙ₊₁ − q·pₙ and a³+b³+c³ = −3q.

overview.historicalContext:
Newton's identities (also called the Newton–Girard formulae) relate the power sums $p_k = \sum_i x_i^k$ of a collection of quantities to their elementary symmetric polynomials $e_1, e_2, \dots$. They were stated by Albert Girard in 1629 (in *Invention nouvelle en l'algèbre*) and developed by Isaac Newton around 1666–1683 (published in the *Arithmetica Universalis*, 1707). Together with Vieta's formulas — which identify the coefficients of a polynomial with the elementary symmetric functions of its roots — they form the computational core of the classical theory of symmetric functions, the precursor of Galois theory.

For three quantities $a, b, c$ with $e_1 = a+b+c$, $e_2 = ab+bc+ca$, $e_3 = abc$, the identities read
  $p_1 = e_1$,
  $p_2 = e_1 p_1 - 2e_2$,
  $p_3 = e_1 p_2 - e_2 p_1 + 3e_3$,
and for $k \ge 4$ the homogeneous three-term recurrence
  $p_k = e_1 p_{k-1} - e_2 p_{k-2} + e_3 p_{k-3}$.
The two regimes unify into a single statement $p_{n+3} = e_1 p_{n+2} - e_2 p_{n+1} + e_3 p_n$ valid for all $n \ge 0$ once one sets $p_0 = 3$ (the number of variables); the apparent anomaly $+3e_3$ in $p_3$ is precisely $e_3 \cdot p_0$.

The parent entry (Vieta's formulas for the Cardano roots) lists 'formalize the Newton–Girard identities expressing power sums in terms of elementary symmetric polynomials' as an explicit open question. This entry answers it for the cubic, and in fact for any three elements of an arbitrary commutative ring.
overview.problemStatement: For three elements a, b, c of a commutative ring with elementary symmetric functions e₁, e₂, e₃, prove that the power sums pₙ = aⁿ+bⁿ+cⁿ satisfy pₙ₊₃ = e₁pₙ₊₂ − e₂pₙ₊₁ + e₃pₙ for every n, derive the closed forms and classical Newton identities for p₁..p₄, and specialize to the depressed cubic x³+px+q of the parent.
overview.proofStrategy: The whole development rests on one observation: each of a, b, c is a root of the monic cubic X³ − e₁X² + e₂X − e₃ = (X−a)(X−b)(X−c), so a³ = e₁a² − e₂a + e₃ — and crucially this is a *ring identity* (the b- and c-terms cancel), provable by `ring`. Multiplying by aⁿ gives aⁿ⁺³ = e₁aⁿ⁺² − e₂aⁿ⁺¹ + e₃aⁿ; the symmetric statements hold for b and c. Summing the three per-root recurrences with `linear_combination` yields the Newton–Girard recurrence directly, with no induction. The low-order closed forms and triangular identities have concrete exponents and follow by `ring`. The depressed-cubic corollaries substitute e₁ = 0, e₂ = p, e₃ = −q.
keyInsights: The engine is a hidden ring identity: a³ = (a+b+c)a² − (ab+bc+ca)a + abc holds because the b- and c-terms cancel, so it is provable by `ring` with no hypothesis that a is a 'root' — yet it IS exactly the statement that a is a root of (X−a)(X−b)(X−c).

Newton–Girard needs no induction here: multiplying the cubic each root satisfies by xⁿ and summing gives the recurrence for all n in one shot. `ring` handles the symbolic exponent n+k by normalizing aⁿ⁺² = aⁿ·a².

The famous +3e₃ in p₃ = e₁p₂ − e₂p₁ + 3e₃ is not a special case at all: it is e₃·p₀ with p₀ = a⁰+b⁰+c⁰ = 3. The 'three' literally counts the variables, unifying the triangular identities with the homogeneous tail.

The recurrence pₙ₊₃ = e₁pₙ₊₂ − e₂pₙ₊₁ + e₃pₙ together with p₀=3, p₁=e₁, p₂=e₁²−2e₂ computes every power sum from the symmetric functions alone — the mechanism by which sums of powers of roots are 'coefficient data'.
Specializing to the parent's depressed cubic (e₁=0) collapses the three-term recurrence to two terms pₙ₊₃ = −p·pₙ₊₁ − q·pₙ, and immediately yields the classical a³+b³+c³ = −3q for roots of x³+px+q.

Working over an arbitrary CommRing rather than ℂ shows the identities are purely formal/algebraic: they hold for indeterminates, integers mod n, matrices over a commutative base, etc., not merely for complex roots.
prerequisites: Elementary symmetric polynomials of three variables
Vieta's formulas relating polynomial coefficients to symmetric functions of the roots
The `ring` and `linear_combination` tactics for commutative-ring identities

sections.title: Section I: Elementary Symmetric Functions and Power Sums
sections.summary: Defines e₁ = a+b+c, e₂ = ab+bc+ca, e₃ = abc, the power sum pₙ = aⁿ+bⁿ+cⁿ, and the base value p₀ = 3.
sections.mathContext: The base case p₀ = 3 counts the number of variables and is exactly the constant that makes the unified recurrence reproduce the +3e₃ term of the third Newton identity.

sections.title: Section II: Each Root Satisfies the Cubic
sections.summary: Proves a³ = e₁a² − e₂a + e₃ (and symmetrically for b, c) — each quantity is a root of X³ − e₁X² + e₂X − e₃, as a pure ring identity.
sections.mathContext: This is the algebraic shadow of Vieta: (X−a)(X−b)(X−c) = X³ − e₁X² + e₂X − e₃, so each of a, b, c annihilates the right-hand side.

sections.title: Section III: Per-Root Recurrences
sections.summary: Multiplying each root's cubic by xⁿ gives xⁿ⁺³ = e₁xⁿ⁺² − e₂xⁿ⁺¹ + e₃xⁿ for x ∈ {a, b, c}.
sections.mathContext: These three single-variable recurrences are the summands whose sum is the Newton–Girard recurrence; `ring` discharges each because it normalizes symbolic exponents.

sections.title: Section IV: The Newton–Girard Recurrence
sections.summary: The main theorem: pₙ₊₃ = e₁pₙ₊₂ − e₂pₙ₊₁ + e₃pₙ for all n, proved by summing the three per-root recurrences via linear_combination; plus the shifted form for the homogeneous range k ≥ 4.
sections.mathContext: A single linear recurrence with constant (symmetric-function) coefficients that, with three initial values, determines all power sums of the three quantities.

sections.title: Section V: Closed Forms and the Triangular Newton Identities
sections.summary: Closed forms p₁=e₁, p₂=e₁²−2e₂, p₃=e₁³−3e₁e₂+3e₃, p₄=e₁⁴−4e₁²e₂+4e₁e₃+2e₂², and the classical triangular identities newton_p1..p4 including p₃ = e₁p₂ − e₂p₁ + 3e₃.
sections.mathContext: The triangular identities are the textbook form of Newton–Girard; the +3e₃ is e₃·p₀, exhibiting p₀ = 3 as the source of the constant.

sections.title: Section VI: Specialization to the Depressed Cubic x³ + px + q
sections.summary: With e₁ = 0, e₂ = p, e₃ = −q (Vieta for the parent's depressed cubic), the recurrence collapses to pₙ₊₃ = −p·pₙ₊₁ − q·pₙ, with p₁ = 0, p₂ = −2p, and the classical sum of cubes a³+b³+c³ = −3q.
sections.mathContext: Directly connects Newton–Girard to the parent: the power sums of the Cardano roots are generated by a two-term recurrence built from the cubic's own coefficients p and q.

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) formalization of the Newton–Girard identities for three quantities over an arbitrary commutative ring, in 219 lines with 21 theorems and 4 definitions. The development hinges on the ring identity a³ = e₁a² − e₂a + e₃ (each quantity is a root of (X−a)(X−b)(X−c)); multiplying by xⁿ and summing yields the recurrence pₙ₊₃ = e₁pₙ₊₂ − e₂pₙ₊₁ + e₃pₙ for all n with no induction, after which the closed forms, triangular identities, and depressed-cubic specialization follow by `ring`/`linear_combination`.
conclusion.implications: This answers the parent entry's open question on Newton–Girard identities and completes the roots↔coefficients dictionary for the cubic: Vieta expresses the symmetric functions as coefficients, Newton–Girard then computes every power sum of the roots from those coefficients. Because everything is proved over an arbitrary commutative ring, the identities apply not just to complex roots but to indeterminates, finite rings, and matrix entries. The unified recurrence with p₀ = 3 clarifies the textbook 'anomaly' of the +3e₃ term, and the depressed-cubic corollary a³+b³+c³ = −3q shows how the abstract recurrence specializes to concrete classical facts.
openQuestions: Generalize to n quantities: prove the general Newton–Girard recurrence pₖ = Σⱼ (−1)ʲ⁺¹ eⱼ pₖ₋ⱼ over an arbitrary commutative ring, ideally bridging to Mathlib's MvPolynomial.esymm / psum and its NewtonIdentities development.
Derive the reverse map (elementary symmetric functions from power sums) over a ℚ-algebra, exhibiting the Newton–Girard system as triangular and invertible when the number of variables is invertible.

crossReferences.description: Parent proof: Vieta's formulas for the Cardano roots. That entry proves the elementary symmetric functions equal the coefficients (σ₁=0, σ₂=p, σ₃=−q) and explicitly lists formalizing the Newton–Girard identities as an open question. This entry answers it, computing every power sum of the roots from the symmetric functions and specializing the recurrence to the depressed cubic via e₁=0, e₂=p, e₃=−q.

Grandparent: Cardano's radical formula for the depressed cubic. The depressed-cubic specialization here (pₙ₊₃ = −p·pₙ₊₁ − q·pₙ and a³+b³+c³ = −3q) describes the power sums of exactly the roots Cardano's formula produces.

Vieta's formulas give the coefficients as elementary symmetric functions of the roots; Newton–Girard completes the dictionary by computing the power sums of the roots from those same symmetric functions. Together they characterize how root data and coefficient data determine one another.

Both are foundational polynomial identities proved by ring normalization. The closed forms for p₂, p₃, p₄ in terms of e₁, e₂, e₃ are the symmetric-function analogues of binomial/multinomial expansions.
